question: We don't always make the right judgment all the time. Tell me about a time when you made an error in judgment. What was the impact? What did you learn? How have you applied what you learned?
competency: Are Right, A Lot (learning from errors in judgment)

raiseTranscript.text: I misestimated the effort on a feature by assuming a library would handle edge cases cleanly. The impact was a two-day slip on a sprint deliverable that affected only my task. I learned to validate assumptions with a quick spike or peer check before committing. Since then I always run a 30-minute proof-of-concept on any new dependency and flag risks in planning.
I had used the library once before on a smaller project and it worked, so I didn't test the specific data shape we had here.

raiseNotes: Q: error in judgment story
Situation: underestimated library edge cases on personal task
Action: now runs quick spike + flags risks
Outcome: prevented repeat slips on own work
Quote: 'I always run a 30-minute proof-of-concept'
Follow-up: assumption source - admitted prior success bias
junior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar on Are Right, A Lot for junior. Candidate owned a narrow scope error that delayed only their task and described a concrete process change they now apply. The quote about running a 30-minute spike shows they turned the mistake into an owned habit rather than a one-off. This demonstrates coachability and local ownership expected at 0-2 years. The follow-up revealed the root cause was prior success bias, which they addressed without external prompting. Biggest strength is the direct link from error to repeatable personal safeguard.

lowerTranscript.text: I picked the wrong approach on a ticket but the team caught it in review so the impact was minimal. I learned to listen more to senior engineers.
It seemed faster at the time and I didn't want to overthink it.

lowerNotes: Situation: wrong approach caught in review
Quote: 'it seemed faster at the time'
Follow-up: reasoning - stayed vague on why it was wrong
junior.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar on Are Right, A Lot for junior. The candidate minimized ownership by crediting the team for catching the issue and gave a generic learning point about listening rather than a specific process change. No measurable impact or before-after behavior was described. The follow-up showed the original judgment was based on speed without analysis. This pattern suggests limited reflection and weak personal ownership, which is below the threshold even for entry level.

raiseTranscript.text: I pushed for a shared service design that two other teams adopted, but it created latency under their load patterns. Impact was a quarter-long performance regression affecting three teams until we added caching. I learned to run cross-team load tests before advocating patterns. Now I require a 48-hour bake with synthetic traffic from each consuming team before any shared component ships.
How did you get the other teams to adopt it initially?
I presented benchmarks from our workload only and assumed similarity.

raiseNotes: Q: error in judgment story
Situation: advocated shared service without cross-team validation
Action: now mandates 48-hour multi-team bake
Outcome: prevented repeat cross-team regressions
Quote: 'require a 48-hour bake with synthetic traffic from each consuming team'
Follow-up: adoption driver - admitted single-workload benchmarks
senior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar on Are Right, A Lot for senior. The candidate described an error with cross-team scope, quantified the quarter-long impact, and implemented a new validation step that now protects multiple teams. The quote shows the learning was turned into an enforceable process rather than personal advice. Follow-up clarified the root cause was assuming workload similarity, which they addressed with broader testing. This level of influence without authority and measurable downstream improvement meets senior expectations.

lowerTranscript.text: I chose a design that didn't scale well for one dependent team. We fixed it after launch. I learned to consider more use cases next time.
What data did you have on their workload?
Mostly what they told us in a single meeting.

lowerNotes: Situation: design didn't scale for dependent team
Quote: 'mostly what they told us in a single meeting'
Follow-up: data source - limited to one conversation
senior.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar on Are Right, A Lot for senior. Impact stayed vague and post-hoc; no metrics or duration were given. The learning remained aspirational without a changed mechanism or evidence of application to other work. Follow-up showed reliance on a single meeting rather than proactive data gathering. This reflects individual-level reflection instead of the cross-team influence and repeatable safeguards expected at senior level.

raiseTranscript.text: I staffed a critical project with a strong but overloaded engineer because I wanted quick delivery. The engineer burned out and two other projects slipped. I learned to run explicit capacity checks with peer managers before committing people. Since then my team has a standing rule that any cross-project staffing requires a written capacity review from the owning manager first.
Through missed milestones and a 1:1 where they admitted working weekends for six weeks.

raiseNotes: Q: error in judgment story
Situation: overloaded key engineer for speed
Action: created written capacity review rule
Outcome: protected team capacity across projects
Quote: 'any cross-project staffing requires a written capacity review'
Follow-up: burnout signal - missed milestones and 1:1 admission
manager.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar on Are Right, A Lot for manager. The candidate owned a staffing judgment that produced team-level burnout and project slippage, then converted the lesson into a durable team process that now involves peer managers. The quote demonstrates leverage through process rather than heroics. Follow-up showed they tracked concrete signals like missed milestones. This reflects the people-development and team-outcome ownership required at manager level.

lowerTranscript.text: I assigned the wrong person to lead a project and had to step in later. I learned to better match skills to projects.
They seemed capable in their prior role.

lowerNotes: Quote: 'seemed capable in their prior role'
Follow-up: missed signals - relied on past role performance
manager.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar on Are Right, A Lot for manager. The story stayed at the level of one assignment without team-wide impact or process change. Learning was stated at a high level with no evidence of application or prevention of recurrence. Follow-up revealed the judgment was based on outdated signals rather than current capacity. This lacks the team-leverage and underperformance-handling focus expected of managers.

raiseTranscript.text: I green-lit an acquisition that looked strategically aligned on paper but whose culture and tech stack proved incompatible. Integration cost exceeded forecast by 40% and two key product lines lost momentum for a year. I learned to run a 90-day cultural and technical due-diligence exercise with joint teams before final approval. That practice is now embedded in our M&A playbook and has been used on the last three deals.
What made the original analysis insufficient?
We modeled synergies but never stress-tested day-to-day operating differences.

raiseNotes: Q: error in judgment story
Situation: acquisition with culture/tech mismatch
Action: embedded 90-day joint due-diligence in M&A playbook
Outcome: applied to last three deals
Quote: 'now embedded in our M&A playbook'
Follow-up: analysis gap - modeled synergies but skipped operating differences
exec.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar on Are Right, A Lot for exec. The candidate described a high-ambiguity strategic error with org-level cost and momentum impact, then institutionalized a new due-diligence step that now governs future decisions. The quote shows long-term leverage through process change rather than one-off correction. Follow-up identified the exact analytical blind spot. This demonstrates strategic judgment and trade-off thinking at the scale expected of execs.

lowerTranscript.text: We made an investment that didn't pan out as expected. We adjusted the strategy afterward. I learned to look at more scenarios.
What was the scale of the miss?
It affected our quarterly numbers but we recovered.

lowerNotes: Quote: 'affected our quarterly numbers but we recovered'
Follow-up: scale - stayed at quarterly level without org impact
exec.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar on Are Right, A Lot for exec. The error was framed at a quarterly financial level without org or multi-year consequences. Learning remained generic without evidence of changed decision frameworks or lasting organizational impact. Follow-up did not surface strategic trade-offs or long-term thinking. This reads as tactical rather than the high-ambiguity, playbook-level judgment required at exec level.

diagnostic.exec: Identifies synergy vs operating model gap
